# II. A Game of Chess

The Chair she sat in, like a burnished throne [**like a burnished throne**: *A direct allusion to Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra (Act II, Scene 2), describing Cleopatra's barge.*]{.aside},
Glowed on the marble, where the glass
Held up by standards wrought with fruited vines
From which a golden Cupidon peeped out
(Another hid his eyes behind his wing)
Doubled the flames of sevenbranched candelabra
Reflecting light upon the table as
The glitter of her jewels rose to meet it,
From satin cases poured in rich profusion.
In vials of ivory and coloured glass
Unstoppered, lurked her strange synthetic perfumes,
Unguent, powdered, or liquid—troubled, confused
And drowned the sense in odours; stirred by the air
That freshened from the window, these ascended
In fattening the prolonged candle-flames,
Flung their smoke into the laquearia [**laquearia**: *A paneled ceiling. The reference is to Virgil's Aeneid (Book I), describing Dido's banquet.*]{.aside},
Stirring the pattern on the coffered ceiling.
Huge sea-wood fed with copper
Burned green and orange, framed by the coloured stone,
In which sad light a carvèd dolphin swam.
Above the antique mantel was displayed
As though a window gave upon the sylvan scene [**sylvan scene**: *A reference to Milton's Paradise Lost (Book IV), describing the Garden of Eden.*]{.aside}
The change of Philomel [**Philomel**: *In Greek mythology, Philomela was raped by Tereus, who cut out her tongue. The gods transformed her into a nightingale.*]{.aside}, by the barbarous king
So rudely forced; yet there the nightingale
Filled all the desert with inviolable voice
And still she cried, and still the world pursues,
"Jug Jug" [**Jug Jug**: *A traditional Elizabethan representation of the nightingale's song, sometimes with crude sexual connotations.*]{.aside} to dirty ears.

*(Excerpt from Section II. The poem continues through Section III "The Fire Sermon", Section IV "Death by Water", and Section V "What the Thunder Said".)*

# III. The Fire Sermon

The river's tent is broken; the last fingers of leaf
Clutch and sink into the wet bank. The wind
Crosses the brown land, unheard. The nymphs are departed.
Sweet Thames, run softly, till I end my song [**Sweet Thames...**: *A refrain from Edmund Spenser's Prothalamion.*]{.aside}.
The river bears no empty bottles, sandwich papers,
Silk handkerchiefs, cardboard boxes, cigarette ends
Or other testimony of summer nights. The nymphs are departed.
And their friends, the loitering heirs of City directors;
Departed, have left no addresses.
By the waters of Leman [**Leman**: *Lake Geneva (Lac Léman) in Switzerland, where Eliot wrote part of the poem while recovering from a breakdown.*]{.aside} I sat down and wept...

# IV. Death by Water

Phlebas the Phoenician, a fortnight dead,
Forgot the cry of gulls, and the deep sea swell
And the profit and loss.
A current under sea
Picked his bones in whispers. As he rose and fell
He passed the stages of his age and youth
Entering the whirlpool.
Gentile or Jew
O you who turn the wheel and look to windward,
Consider Phlebas, who was once handsome and tall as you.

# V. What the Thunder Said

After the torchlight red on sweaty faces
After the frosty silence in the gardens
After the agony in stony places
The shouting and the crying
Prison and palace and reverberation
Of thunder of spring over distant mountains
He who was living is now dead
We who were living are now dying
With a little patience

*(The poem concludes with the Sanskrit words "Shantih shantih shantih" [**Shantih**: *A formal ending to an Upanishad, translated by Eliot as "The Peace which passeth understanding."*]{.aside}.)*
